labs.title: Missing Signer Check
labs.concept: In Solana, nothing stops anyone from passing any account as "authority". If the handler never calls `is_signer`, a stranger can invoke privileged actions as someone else — no signature required. The single most common root cause in Solana exploits.
labs.realWorld: Class behind countless drains; the pack proved it on our own vault corpus — 5 SOL gone in one tx.

labs.title: Account Data Matching
labs.concept: An account that is structurally right but semantically wrong: the type checks out, the data inside belongs to someone else. Without checking a stored field (e.g. `account.authority == signer.key`), the program trusts whatever was passed.
labs.realWorld: Variant of the Cashio infinite-mint: an unvalidated collateral account let the attacker mint $52M of CASH.

labs.title: Owner Checks
labs.concept: Any program can create an account with any bytes in it. If you deserialize an AccountInfo without checking `account.owner == expected_program`, an attacker crafts a fake account that parses perfectly and drains the vault.
labs.realWorld: Owner-check bypass = the "fake account" primitive behind most pre-Anchor exploits; Anchor `Account<T>` does it for you — AccountInfo never does.

labs.title: Type Cosplay
labs.concept: Two account structs with identical layout but different meaning. Pass account B where A is expected: fields reinterpreted, authority fields become balances. Anchor fixes this with the 8-byte discriminator — raw Solana programs must roll their own.
labs.realWorld: The reason Anchor prepends a type discriminator to every account — without it, bytes are just bytes.

labs.title: Reinitialization
labs.concept: An `init`-style instruction callable twice on the same account resets authority/data to attacker-controlled values. `init_if_needed` is the classic footgun: "needed" is decided by the caller, and a re-init overwrites the admin.
labs.realWorld: Reinit bugs killed several early Solana protocols; Anchor 0.25+ made `init_if_needed` require explicit opt-in flags for a reason.

labs.title: Arbitrary CPI
labs.concept: `invoke`/`invoke_signed` trust the program_id account passed in. If it isn't pinned to an expected address, the attacker supplies their own program — which happily reports "transfer succeeded" while keeping the tokens.
labs.realWorld: The pack CONFIRMED this class on sealevel-attacks: invoke with arbitrary program id + signer-bit propagation = real drain.

labs.title: Duplicate Mutable Accounts
labs.concept: Pass the same account twice in the accounts array and the runtime hands your handler two mutable references to one account. Debit it as "A" and "B" — you just debited twice the same balance.
labs.realWorld: Classic double-spend primitive; the fix is a one-line key equality check Anchor does via constraints.

labs.title: Bump Seed Canonicalization
labs.concept: A PDA can be derived with multiple valid bumps, but only one is canonical. Accepting a non-canonical bump lets an attacker derive a second address for the "same" PDA — two accounts where the program expects one.
labs.realWorld: Subtle but real: non-canonical PDAs break the one-account-one-vault invariant protocols rely on.

labs.title: PDA Sharing
labs.concept: Reusing one PDA as the authority for many things (vault + mint + pool) means any instruction that can sign with it controls all of them. Seeds should encode domain + instance: one PDA, one job.
labs.realWorld: Over-powered PDAs turn one buggy instruction into total protocol control.

labs.title: Closing Accounts & Revival
labs.concept: Marking an account closed (lamports → 0) is not enough: a later instruction in the same tx can "revive" it by refunding rent, leaving a zeroed-but-live account ready for reinit. The exit writeback stomps the zeroing — the pack confirmed revival survives every "fixed" variant.
labs.realWorld: The pack found an inverted check in the "secure" variant of this lesson — a real upstream bug in the teaching repo itself.

labs.title: Sysvar Address Checking
labs.concept: Before `sysvar::instructions` became a real syscall, the instruction sysvar was just an account — and attackers passed a fake one to forge instruction introspection. Always pin sysvar accounts to their known addresses.
labs.realWorld: Wormhole lost $326M to a forged sysvar account — the largest bridge exploit in crypto started exactly here.
